sections.section_name: Section B - Very Short Structural Functions

questions.question_text: Identify the primary biological function of the Leydig cells located within the interstitial spaces of the human testis architecture. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: Leydig cells synthesize and secrete testicular hormones called androgens, primarily testosterone, which regulate spermatogenesis and maintain secondary sexual characteristics.

questions.question_text: Briefly describe the structural outcome of the double fertilization event specific to angiosperms, identifying the two fusion products. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: Double fertilization yields a diploid zygote via syngamy (fusion of sperm and egg) and a triploid primary endosperm nucleus (PEN) via triple fusion, which nourishes the embryo.

questions.question_text: Differentiate between the concepts of a test cross and a back cross in classical Mendelian genetic frameworks. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: A test cross involves mating an $F_1$ hybrid specifically with a homozygous recessive parent to determine genotype. A back cross mates an $F_1$ hybrid with either parental type.

questions.question_text: State the essential biological role of the enzyme aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase during the initiation phase of translation. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: This enzyme catalyzes the specific attachment of an amino acid to its corresponding tRNA molecule, utilizing ATP energy, effectively "charging" the tRNA for peptide bond formation.

questions.question_text: Explain the concept of homologous structures using the forelimbs of mammals as a primary evolutionary example. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: Homologous structures share a common anatomical plan due to shared ancestry but perform different functions. Mammalian forelimbs share bone structure but adapt for flying, swimming, or running.

questions.question_text: Describe the physiological process of spermatogenesis in human males, highlighting the distinct cellular stages from spermatogonia to mature spermatozoa. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: Diploid spermatogonia multiply via mitosis. Some mature into primary spermatocytes, undergoing meiosis I to form haploid secondary spermatocytes. Meiosis II produces four haploid spermatids, which differentiate structurally into motile spermatozoa during spermiogenesis.

questions.question_text: Outline the essential structural components and functional regions of a typical mature angiosperm embryo sac just prior to fertilization. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: The mature embryo sac is 7-celled and 8-nucleate. It contains a 3-celled egg apparatus (one egg, two synergids) at the micropylar end, three antipodal cells at the chalazal end, and a central cell with two polar nuclei.

questions.question_text: Explain the phenomenon of incomplete dominance using the flower color inheritance pattern of the snapdragon plant (Antirrhinum sp.) as a model. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: Crossing a homozygous red flower ($RR$) with a homozygous white ($rr$) yields an $F_1$ generation with pink flowers ($Rr$). Neither allele is completely dominant, producing an intermediate phenotype where the phenotypic and genotypic ratios match at 1:2:1.

questions.question_text: Detail the continuous and discontinuous replication processes occurring at the replication fork, identifying the specific enzymes managing the lagging strand. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: DNA Polymerase synthesizes the leading strand continuously in the $5' \rightarrow 3'$ direction. The lagging strand is synthesized discontinuously into Okazaki fragments, which are subsequently sealed together by the enzyme DNA ligase to form a complete strand.

questions.question_text: Describe the principle of natural selection as demonstrated by the industrial melanism observed in the peppered moth population of England. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: Before industrialization, light-colored moths survived predation on pale lichens. Post-industrial pollution darkened tree trunks, shifting survival advantage to dark-colored (melanic) mutants, demonstrating natural selection favoring traits adaptive to the changed environment.

questions.question_text: Clarify the precise biological mechanism by which the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) compromises the human immune system leading to AIDS. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: HIV selectively infects and destroys helper T-lymphocytes ($T_H$ cells) using reverse transcription to replicate its viral RNA. The progressive depletion of $T_H$ cells cripples the immune response, leaving the body vulnerable to severe opportunistic infections.

questions.question_text: Explain the structural basis and inheritance pattern of sickle-cell anaemia as an autosomal recessive genetic disorder. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: A point mutation substitutes valine for glutamic acid at the 6th position of the beta-globin chain. This structural defect causes RBCs to become sickle-shaped under low oxygen. Individuals must inherit two defective alleles ($Hb^S Hb^S$) to exhibit the disease.

questions.question_text: Read the following case context: A geneticist traces the inheritance of a specific trait through a family pedigree over three generations. The trait appears equally in both males and females. However, unaffected parents produce an affected offspring. Identify the precise mode of inheritance for this trait and outline the genotypic configuration of the carrier parents. [40-50 words]
questions.answer: The appearance of an affected offspring from unaffected parents confirms the trait is recessive. Equal distribution among sexes indicates it is autosomal. Therefore, the mode is autosomal recessive. Both unaffected parents must be heterozygous carriers (e.g., $Aa$), passing the recessive allele ($a$) to the affected offspring ($aa$).

questions.question_text: Read the following case context: An experiment investigates the DNA transforming principle using Streptococcus pneumoniae bacteria. Heat-killed virulent (S) strain is mixed with live non-virulent (R) strain and injected into mice. The mice die, and live S strain is recovered. Identify the scientist who performed this experiment, explain the molecular transformation observed, and state the final biological conclusion. [40-50 words]
questions.answer: Frederick Griffith conducted this experiment. The live R strain bacteria assimilated the genetic material from the heat-killed S strain, transforming them structurally into a virulent, capsule-producing S strain. This proved that a "transforming principle" transferred genetic information, later identified physically as DNA.

sections.section_name: Section E - Comprehensive Essays & Labeled Diagrams

questions.question_text: Explain the complete process of the human menstrual cycle, detailing the distinct ovarian and uterine phases coordinated by specific pituitary and ovarian hormonal surges. Include a description of the structural changes in the endometrium. [50-60 words]
questions.answer: The cycle begins with the menstrual phase involving endometrial breakdown. The follicular phase follows, where FSH stimulates follicle maturation and estrogen thickens the endometrium. An LH surge triggers ovulation. The luteal phase sees the corpus luteum secrete progesterone, highly vascularizing the endometrium for potential implantation. Without fertilization, progesterone drops, initiating menstruation.

questions.question_text: Detail the structural steps of the transcription process in prokaryotes, highlighting the specific roles of RNA polymerase and associated initiation/termination factors. Clarify why post-transcriptional modifications are generally absent in this pathway. [50-60 words]
questions.answer: Transcription initiates when RNA polymerase binds the promoter, assisted by the sigma ($\sigma$) factor. During elongation, the enzyme synthesizes mRNA in a $5' \rightarrow 3'$ direction. Termination occurs when the enzyme hits a terminator sequence, utilizing the rho ($\rho$) factor to release the nascent RNA. Modifications are absent because prokaryotic genes lack introns, and translation begins simultaneously.

questions.question_text: Describe the structural layout and molecular regulation of the lac operon in Escherichia coli in the presence and absence of the inducer molecule (lactose). Explain the physiological necessity of this genetic switch. [50-60 words]
questions.answer: In the absence of lactose, the repressor protein binds the operator region, physically blocking RNA polymerase and preventing transcription of structural genes ($z, y, a$). When lactose (inducer) is present, it binds the repressor, altering its structure so it cannot bind the operator. Transcription proceeds, producing enzymes required for lactose metabolism, ensuring metabolic energy efficiency.
